solutions.check: 29 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Pot starts to wise up politician, a self-important type

indicators.note: the starts of words are their opening letters, so only those are kept from the next two words

blocks.note: a mug is a drinking pot
the opening letters of these two words
Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A pompous politician is advised to drink up and get wise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pot' looks like cannabis or a belly, but it is just a mug.
explanation.definitionFit: A mugwump is an old American term for a person who holds aloof and thinks highly of himself, especially in politics.

clue.text: Maybe Alice's coming over topless old German artist

indicators.note: without its top, the name loses its first letter, which sits at the top of a down entry

blocks.note: an advent is an arrival or coming
Albrecht Dürer, the Renaissance painter and engraver

explanation.surface: Someone called Alice seems to be arriving on top of a long-dead German painter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Alice's' is read as 'Alice is'; in a down entry the first piece sits over the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Lewis Carroll's heroine stars in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, so she is an example of a bold explorer.

clue.text: Cold bollocks? Check genital area

blocks.note: C is the tap abbreviation for cold
bollocks is British slang for nonsense, as is rot
CH is the chess abbreviation for check

explanation.surface: A man with chilly testicles is told to inspect himself down below.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bollocks' looks anatomical, which suits the surface, but here it means nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: The crotch is the part of the body where the legs meet, around the genitals.

clue.text: see 14dn.
Drink present in second testicle

indicators.note: one thing set in another is held inside it, so these letters go within the rest

blocks.note: the present moment is now
S for second, and ball as slang for a testicle

explanation.surface: Someone finds a strange gift lodged in their other testicle.
explanation.definitionFit: A snowball is a cocktail of advocaat and lemonade, a Christmas favourite in Britain.

clue.text: see 16dn.
Mince pies piss off reps

indicators.note: food gone off has spoiled, so these letters are spoilt into a new order

blocks.note: both mean urine or to urinate
taken as written

explanation.surface: Mince pies are rude enough to tell the sales reps to go away.
explanation.walkthrough: In Cockney rhyming slang 'mince pies' are eyes, and 'piss off' looks like a single dismissal but splits into two jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: Peepers is jokey slang for eyes, which is what mince pies stands for in rhyming slang.

clue.text: Don't spy on park shaggers enough to be a likely  loser?

definitions.text: Don't spy on park shaggers enough

blocks.clueFragment: Don't spy on park shaggers enough
blocks.note: dogging is watching couples have sex in car parks
the competitor not expected to win

explanation.surface: A lazy voyeur's failure to watch enough outdoor sex marks him out as a probable failure.
explanation.walkthrough: Dogging is British slang for watching or having sex in a public car park; the first half reads the answer as the verb 'under-dog'.
explanation.definitionFit: An underdog is the competitor expected to lose a contest.

clue.text: Archer tale may well be turn off  – upset whole bloc of countries

indicators.note: something off is wrong or out of order, so these letters are rearranged
upset means tipped over, so the abbreviation is turned back to front

blocks.note: taken as written
the European Union

explanation.surface: A jibe at Jeffrey Archer's stories, mixed with someone being put off and annoying the whole of Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: Jeffrey Archer is a novelist and Tory peer jailed for perjury, so a tale of his may well be false.
explanation.definitionFit: Untrue means false, which is the dig at a convicted perjurer's stories.

clue.text: Ill-conceived as Britain's premier consumed by unbridled egotism

indicators.note: the premier letter is the first one, so only the opening of that word is kept
unbridled means running wild, so the letters break loose into a new order
what is consumed ends up inside the eater, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: the first letter of the word
taken as written

explanation.surface: A jab at a prime minister swallowed up by his own unchecked vanity.
explanation.definitionFit: Misbegot is an old form of misbegotten, meaning badly planned or illegitimately conceived.

clue.text: It's corny, the end of Labourite in question

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, which is all that is kept
one thing in another sits inside it, so the single letter goes within the other word

blocks.note: what is a question word
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A Labour politician's question is dismissed as hackneyed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corny' looks like a sneer at a stale joke, but it means made of corn.
explanation.definitionFit: Wheat is a cereal crop, and in Britain corn is the general name for such grain.

clue.text: Cyclops get stuck into awful pushy twat endlessly seen on the box?

indicators.note: without its end, the last word loses its final letter
something awful is a mess, so these letters are jumbled
to get stuck into something is to be lodged inside it

blocks.note: the setter speaking of himself, as I
taken as written

explanation.surface: The setter vows to lay into a dreadful pushy idiot who never stops appearing on TV.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The box' looks like television, but it is a cardboard box with a label on it.
explanation.definitionFit: The words printed on a packing case tell handlers which side must face upward.

clue.text: Familiar ex-Tory MP hack, tense inside: "What, me outed?"

indicators.note: outed means turned out, so these letters are turned into a new order
inside puts the single letter within the reworked letters

blocks.note: taken as written
T is the grammar abbreviation for tense

explanation.surface: A former Tory MP turned journalist nervously asks whether he is the one being outed.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition and the 'outed' both point to Matthew Parris, a former Conservative MP turned columnist who was outed as gay; 'familiar' asks for his first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Matthew Parris, ex-Conservative MP and newspaper columnist, is known familiarly by his first name.

clue.text: (& 4dn.) Punishing location – Nick needs fix and good support

blocks.note: to nick and to whip both mean to steal
to pin something is to fix it in place
G is the abbreviation for good
a post is an upright support

explanation.surface: A police station needs repairs and proper backing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nick' looks like the police station, which suits 'location', but it is the verb meaning steal.
explanation.definitionFit: A whipping post was the upright stake where offenders were tied to be flogged.

clue.text: Shaking trouser snake first, our retiring cocky type

indicators.note: retiring means withdrawing, so those letters leave the word they sit in
shaking jumbles things up, so what is left is put in a new order

blocks.note: a boa is a large snake
taken as written
taken as written, and removed

explanation.surface: A cocky man waggles his trouser snake while ours shyly withdraws.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trouser snake' reads as one slang phrase for a penis, but the two words do separate jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: A boaster brags, and cocky means arrogantly self-confident.

clue.text: (& 6dn.) Chinese figures inscrutably unmoved by the views of the masses

definitions.text: Chinese figures inscrutably unmoved by the views of the masses

blocks.clueFragment: Chinese figures inscrutably unmoved by the views of the masses
blocks.note: surface reading: Chinese leaders impassively ignoring public opinion
setter's reading: a mass of clay soldiers, unmoving statues that cannot see the crowds who view them

explanation.walkthrough: 'Figures' looks like officials or statistics, but means sculpted figures; the masses are both the crowd of tourists and the multitude of soldiers.
explanation.definitionFit: The thousands of clay soldiers buried with China's first emperor at Xi'an are statues, so they stand impassive before the visiting crowds.

clue.text: Hair, in a funny way, is our Brian's long-desired high point?

blocks.note: the stock jokey phrase for a person's hair
Private Eye calls Prince Charles Brian, and his long-awaited peak would be his coronation

explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye nicknames Prince Charles 'Brian', who waited decades to be crowned; the phrase also means a supreme achievement.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's hair is proverbially her crowning glory, and for an heir the crowning is the triumph he has long awaited.

clue.text: Appropriate retirement place for a 'wet'?

blocks.note: surface reading: where a moderate Tory, a 'wet', might go when he leaves politics
setter's reading: retiring is going to bed, and a bed suited to something wet is one filled with liquid

explanation.walkthrough: A 'wet' was Thatcher's word for a soft-line Conservative; retirement here is going to bed for the night.
explanation.definitionFit: A mattress filled with water is a fitting place for a 'wet' to retire at night.

clue.text: Man, say, first off, is full of empty talk (Sting)

indicators.note: with its first letter off, the island name is cut at the front
something full of another thing holds it inside

blocks.note: the Isle of Man, an example of an island
wind is hot air, idle chatter

explanation.surface: Someone sneers that the singer Sting is a man full of hot air.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed 'Sting' looks like the rock star, but it is the definition meaning a con.
explanation.definitionFit: A sting is slang for a confidence trick, which is a fraud or cheat.

clue.text: Ex-political interviewer in boxers, it being a hot time?

indicators.note: the interviewer is placed in, that is inside, the other word

blocks.note: boxers are a breed of dog
Sir Robin Day, the late BBC political interviewer

explanation.surface: An old political broadcaster sweats in his boxer shorts on a hot day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boxers' looks like underpants, but means the dog breed; Robin Day was a famous British TV political interviewer.
explanation.definitionFit: The dog days are the sultry weeks of high summer, named after the Dog Star rising.

clue.text: US counter's 'Labour' T-shirt?

blocks.note: labour is work
a T-shirt is a kind of top

explanation.surface: An American political campaigner wears a Labour Party T-shirt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'US counter' is not an American activist but the American word for a kitchen surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Americans say counter for the kitchen surface that British people call a worktop.

clue.text: Limitless bank returns with Balls' party – twister!

indicators.note: with no limits, the word loses both ends and keeps only its middle
returning means going back, so these letters run in the opposite direction

blocks.note: the inner letters of the word
balls is slang for nonsense, as is rot
a do is a party

explanation.surface: A bank's profits and Ed Balls's Labour Party are caught in a political whirlwind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Balls' looks like Ed Balls, Labour's shadow chancellor at the time, but it is slang for nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: A twister is American slang for a tornado, from the spinning funnel of wind.

clue.text: Clegg's first one to be entertained by corrupt peer – the makings of a fool?

indicators.note: the first of the name is its opening letter, the only one kept
corrupt means debased or spoilt, so these letters are scrambled
a guest entertained by a host is taken in, so these letters go inside

blocks.note: the opening letter of the name
the Roman numeral for one
taken as written

explanation.surface: Nick Clegg is wined and dined by a crooked lord, which shows what a mug he is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fool' looks like an insult for Clegg, but it is the dessert of fruit and cream.
explanation.definitionFit: A recipe lists the ingredients and method, so it holds what is needed to make a pudding.

clue.text: Unrestricted feature of air guitarist?

blocks.note: first meaning: with no conditions attached
second meaning: someone miming a guitar has no instrument at all

explanation.walkthrough: The second half is read literally: the air guitar has nothing to pluck.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom for an arrangement with no conditions is literally true of an imaginary guitar.

clue.text: see 29ac.
Over which the underworld jams broadcast

indicators.note: broadcast words are heard rather than read, so the spelling follows the spoken form

blocks.note: jams as a verb: gets stuck, sticks

explanation.surface: Criminal gangsters are interfering with radio signals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Underworld' looks like organised crime, but it is the Greek land of the dead.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the Styx is the river the dead cross to reach Hades, so the underworld lies over it.

clue.text: Russell gets end away on date for the press

indicators.note: the end is taken away, so the name drops its final letter

blocks.note: Russell Crowe, the actor
D is the abbreviation for date

explanation.surface: The actor Russell Crowe has sex on a date, as reported in the papers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gets his end away' is British slang for having sex; here the end of the name is taken away.
explanation.definitionFit: A press is a dense throng of people, and so is a crowd.

clue.text: Hint: Brenda gives head

blocks.note: a lead is a clue or hint
Private Eye calls the Queen Brenda, and ER is her royal cipher

explanation.surface: A rumour that the Queen performs oral sex.
explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye's nickname for the Queen is Brenda; ER is Elizabeth Regina.
explanation.definitionFit: The head of a group or organisation is its chief, the person in charge.

clue.text: (& 25dn.) Jump, for pity's sake!

blocks.note: pity and sympathy are both compassion for another's plight
jump and shag are both British slang for having sex

explanation.surface: An exasperated plea for someone to leap, for heaven's sake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For pity's sake' looks like impatience but gives the motive literally; the whole clue doubles as the definition, with the pieces read in reverse order.
explanation.definitionFit: The slang phrase names sex granted out of compassion rather than desire, exactly what the clue describes.
